candidates.lead: Manchester Airport Group boss Chris Woodroofe responds to criticism over parking charges
candidates.evidence_text: Airport boss defends £453m car parking income - BBC News Image caption, Chris Woodroofe said about a third of Manchester Airports Group income is from parking By Roger Johnson , North West and Lynette Horsburgh , North West Published 16 minutes ago The boss of Manchester Airport has defended car parking charges there, arguing they are "competitive". Chris Woodroofe was responding to a customer who asked how the airport can justify more than £150 charge for parking for two weeks. The managing director said the cost was "exactly the same sort of charge" as parking in a town centre for the day, but some customers have said they felt the chanrges were unreasonable. Manchester Airports Group (MAG) - which also includes London Stansted and East Midlands Airports - recently recorded it had made £453m from parking, about a third of its income. Woodroofe told BBC North West Tonight : "If you go into the town centre and look to park for a day in the town centre and do that comparison with the £150 for two weeks, it's exactly the same sort of charge." He said the airport was competing with Uber and taxi firms as well as other parking firms. "The car parking world is a competitive one. We are not the only suppliers of car parking in this market place. There are several other competitors, and so it operates a competitive market place." Image source, Manchester Airport Image caption, Chris Woodroofe said Manchester Airport's drop off charges was the lowest charge of any of the big airports across the UK However, he said comparing the cost of parking in a town centre for a day "isn't really like-for-like". Airport customer Ray McGee told the BBC: "Nobody would realistically be parking their car in a city centre continuously for two weeks, so I don't think that comparison demonstrates the airport charge is reasonable or competitive". Woodroofe said the income generated from parking goes into both the running of the airport and investment. Woodroofe added: "One of the things we'll look to invest in in the future will be another big multi-story car park because there is really high demand for that car parking." When asked if that will bring prices down, he said: "We're always going to operate in a world where we are pricing our car parking in a competitive marketplace." He added the drop off charges at Manchester Airport - which is £5.50 for five minutes - was "the lowest charge of any of the big airports across the UK". candidates.summary: The project forms part of plans to build around 2,000 homes in the wider area

candidates.lead: The project forms part of plans to build around 2,000 homes in the wider area
candidates.evidence_text: Oldham housing estate could be built in "beautiful" valley - BBC News Image source, IDPartnership Image caption, The development is a part of plans to build 2,000 homes in the area By Ed Barnes Local Democracy Reporting Service Published 2 hours ago Nearly 200 homes could be built in a "beautiful" valley as part of a major development that includes a new tram stop. Barratt Homes Manchester have asked Oldham Council to approve up to 192 homes at Birshaw Farm in the Beal Valley, Oldham, Greater Manchester. It forms part of wider plans for the area, which includes around 2,000 homes, as well as other infrastructure. There is also a new road planned from Ripponden Road to Oldham Road, as well as a new Metrolink stop at Broadbent Moss. The scheme is part of the Greater Manchester Places for Everyone scheme, which aims to oversee house building, create jobs, and protect the regions's green belt land from unplanned development. The new homes would be built about three miles north of Oldham town centre and includes an area of greenfield land on the edge of Royton. The development will include wetland landscapes, green spaces, as well as accessible walking and cycling routes according to the plans , external . Image source, IDPartnership Image caption, The developers said the project would deliver £36.7m of gross value to the area Despite the loss of farmland to development, a report said the development will keep "existing woodland and mature tree groupings to establish a distinctive landscape character" with an aim to plant 551 new trees. The vision is to "create welcoming, well-connected neighbourhoods that feel part of the existing communities in Shaw, Royton, Heyside and Barrowshaw," the Local Democracy Reporting Service said. Developers also said the project would deliver 100 direct construction jobs and £36.7m of gross value added to the area. If the homes are built, they said an extra £5.5m would be spent by the homes each year with an extra £500,000 of council tax revenue. 'Irreplaceable landscape' However, concerns have already been raised in a number of comments on Oldham's planning portal. One person said: "Long-standing residents like my husband and me have intentionally stayed here for over 30 years precisely because of the strong community cohesion and the exceptional greenery of the Beal Valley. "By sacrificing this irreplaceable landscape for developer profit, the council is actively destroying the very assets that make Oldham a desirable place to live," they said. "If you take this away, there is no reason for dedicated residents to stay." candidates.lead: Cheadle Royal Hospital's child and adolescent mental health wards are now rated good by inspectors
candidates.evidence_text: Cheadle mental health wards ordered to improve upgraded to 'good' - BBC News Image source, PA Media Image caption, Inspectors carried out tours of two wards as part of the inspection By Lynette Horsburgh North West Published 1 hour ago Child and adolescent mental health wards at a Greater Manchester hospital that had been ordered to improve has been rated as "good" by health inspectors. The Care Quality Commission (CQC) has upgraded the rating of the service at Cheadle Royal Hospital's child and adolescent mental health wards after an inspection in April. The hospital, run by Affinity Healthcare Limited, provides a range of inpatient mental health services for young people between 11-17 and adults. The inspection followed the receipt of information of concern, the CQC said. CQC inspectors found the hospital had made necessary improvements and was now only in breach of one regulation related to safe care and treatment. At the previous inspection, inspectors found five breaches of regulation. At the time of this latest review, the CQC said there were six young people admitted to the main ward and one young person in long-term segregation on another ward, which was not in general use. Inspectors carried out a tour of the Woodlands and Featherstone wards as well as the clinic room and the ward seclusion suite. The CQC upgraded its rating for how responsive and well-led the service was from "required improvement" to "good", and has again rated how effective and caring the service is as good. The report found: Staff treated young people with compassion and kindness, respected their privacy and dignity and involved them and their families in planning their care Leaders had a good understanding of how the ward was run and were visible and approachable to both staff and young people The ward met people's needs well as staff, managed people's cases effectively, they did not move young people between wards unnecessarily and they supported people to leave hospital as soon as they were well enough to do so Staff supported young people with discharge planning, working closely with community teams and commissioners to help them move on to suitable placements. Staff assessed young people's physical and mental health needs thoroughly on admission and reviewed their care plans regularly to reflect any changes. However the inspectors also noted: Staff did not always store medicines safely, putting some young people at risk of receiving medicines that were out of date or had not been stored at the correct temperature Staff did not always update risk records quickly enough after incidents so important information about a young person's specific risks did not always appear in their care plan Some issues with maintenance and infection prevention and control issues in the care environment The CQC has asked Affinity Healthcare Limited for an action plan in response to the concerns found at this assessment. The health watchdog's overall rating at Cheadle Royal Hospital has remained the same as "requires improvement". candidates.lead: The former Manchester United player banned after speeding twice in two days
candidates.evidence_text: Ex Man-Utd player Paul Scholes banned from driving - BBC News Image source, Reuters Image caption, Former Man Utd player Paul Scholes has been for speeding in his Range Rover Published 18 August 2026 Former Manchester United footballer Paul Scholes has been handed a six-month road ban after he racked up two driving convictions in the space of two days. The 51-year-old was caught speeding in a Range Rover on the evening of 3 March while on a late-night drive through Cleckheaton in West Yorkshire. In the second case, Scholes's Mercedes broke the speed limit on Mossley Road near Ashton-under-Lyne, Greater Manchester, on the morning of 14 November last year. On 12 August at Bradford Magistrates' Court, he was handed a six-month driving ban for the first offence, along with fines. The next day at Manchester Magistrates' Court he received six penalty points on his licence, and further fines. Fines, costs, and court fees for the criminal cases totalled £1,472. A court official said Scholes, who was prosecuted in private hearings under the Single Justice Procedure, did not enter pleas to either of the charges he faced and was convicted in his absence. Image source, PA Media Image caption, Scholes was convicted under the Single Justice Procedure Court documents obtained by the Press Association news agency show Scholes's Range Rover was caught speeding at just after 23:30 BST on 3 March on the A649 Halifax Road near Cleckheaton. Police said the former footballer replied to a notice of intended prosecution, confirming he had been the driver. And the court papers noted that Scholes could not be offered the chance of an out-of-court settlement with a speed awareness course as he is a "totter" – meaning he already had penalty points on his licence and was now in line for an automatic ban. In the second case, Scholes's Mercedes broke the speed limit on the A670 Mossley Road near Ashton-under-Lyne at 11:10 BST on 14 November last year. Police said two letters were sent to his home and "no reply has been received". At court, the force dropped the speeding allegation but continued to prosecute Scholes for failing to reply to the letters. Scholes played 499 times for Manchester United and won 66 England caps in a trophy-laden career which included 11 Premier League titles, three FA Cup wins, and two Champions League triumphs. candidates.summary: Victim Support helped Trish through court proceedings after sexual abuse she suffered as a child

candidates.lead: Victim Support helped Trish through court proceedings after sexual abuse she suffered as a child
candidates.evidence_text: Droylsden dad boxes to raise £2k after charity helped his wife - BBC News Image source, Craig Hinde Image caption, Craig says seeing Trish go through the court process made him want to give something back to Victim Support By Haider Saleem North West Published 18 August 2026 A father who had never boxed has raised £2,630 for a charity supporting people affected by crime - after it helped his wife through court proceedings over sexual abuse she suffered as a child. Craig Hinde, 41, from Droylsden, Greater Manchester, trained for eight weeks before taking part in a white-collar boxing event in Manchester. His wife Trish said Victim Support prepared her for court after she reported being sexually abused as a child by her father, Gerard King, who was convicted at Chester Crown Court in 2022. Craig also said it had helped their son Jacob, 10, who took up boxing after being bullied, regain his sparring confidence, showing how trying mattered more than winning. Trish, 38, said she had never been in a courtroom before and described the prospect as "terrifying". The lettings administrator said Victim Support talked her through what to expect and reassured her that it was acceptable to say she did not know or could not remember an answer. "For people who have been through trauma, they often are terrified of not being believed," she said. But she said there was none of that feeling when speaking to the charity. "It's just acceptance and validation," she said. "There's no judgment. They just help you through the process." Image source, Craig Hinde Image caption, Craig said he had avoided physical exercise since injuring his knees at 17 Trish said getting help was "the best thing I ever did" and that she was now a very different person from the one who had gone through the court process. She said hearing somebody acknowledge how awful her experience had been changed the way she thought about what had happened. "For somebody to just say, what happened to you was awful, it just changes something in your brain," she said. Craig said watching his wife go through the case had been extremely difficult: "There's not much I could do, like it was out of my hands" he said. Craig said he had not known about Victim Support until his family needed its help. "You don't know you need them until you need them," he said. He said the charity told him it had "never done this before" when he approached it about raising money through white-collar boxing. Craig said he initially thought raising £50 or £100 would be a good result, but eventually collected £2,630 and was named the event's Golden Glove Top Fundraiser. He trained at ISAN Gym in Oldham and said he had never boxed before signing up. Image source, Craig Hinde Image caption, Craig and Trish say they noticed Jacob's confidence in boxing improve after his father's challenge Craig said Jacob had taken up boxing and the sport had helped him through bullying. However, his son later became hesitant about sparring and Craig wanted to show him that putting himself in an uncomfortable situation was an achievement regardless of whether he won. Jacob was too young to attend the event, but Craig said he showed him footage afterwards. Craig narrowly lost the contest but said: "It was just the getting in there that counted." He said he noticed "a big switch" in Jacob's confidence in the following weeks and that his son had since started technical sparring. Image source, Craig Hinde Image caption, Trish says she was proud that Victim Support was the first charity Craig thought of when deciding where the money should go Craig's training also coincided with the deaths of both his grandparents within days of each other. He said his grandmother died on a Saturday and his grandfather, whom he described as a role model, died the following Monday. Craig said he sat crying in his car before that evening's training session and questioned whether to go inside. "I got tears in the car before I got in there, wiped them," he said. He decided to train and said afterwards: "My head just felt lighter." Craig said the exercise helped him mentally during what he described as "a real difficult time". He said he had been more nervous about the ring walk than the contest itself, but seeing Trish in the crowd had helped. Reflecting on their family life since the court case, Trish said: "We live very much in the moment now." "We try and enjoy every moment." The Met Office says up to 23mm of rain fell in parts of the North West in the 12 hours up to 6am this morning (August 19) It comes as parts of the country are seeing their 'first meaningful rain for a long time' this week, forecasters say. A dry summer has seen repeat heatwaves across the country, with drought conditions in more than two-thirds of England Temperatures have plummeted this week though, with cooler conditions expected through to next week. The Met Office is forecasting highs of 19C in Greater Manchester today, followed by 18C on Thursday, Friday and Saturday Lows could drop to 9C in parts of the region on Thursday and Saturday night. Showers are forecast today and tomorrow, according to the Met Office The heaviest showers are expected to fall around 11am and 7pm today, and throughout Thursday morning. Friday, Saturday and Sunday are expected to be drier, with sunny intervals - although showers could fall between 3pm and 8pm on Friday

candidates.evidence_text: Courts Man's drunken, sweary tirade on Jet2 flight before 300 passengers had 'holidays ruined' "I can say whatever I want, it's a free country - if I think you're a Nazi, I'll say it" Comments News Amy Walker Court reporter 19:18, 18 Aug 2026 View 3 I A drunken man's sweary tirade at cabin crew saw over three hundred people's holiday's 'ruined' as a Jet2 flight was cancelled Jason Mulhern, 57, and his wife, were due to fly to Dalaman, in Turkey, from Manchester Airport , on June 22, 2024, when she made a comment about a fellow passenger's accent As he joined in and began 'shouting', cabin staff spoke to them both, after which they were told they would not be served alcohol. Mulhern, of Trafford , then became 'aggressive, defensive and angry', Manchester Crown Court heard He told staff they were 'out of order', that he and his wife were 'on their holidays' and wanted to 'booze up'. They were spoken to again, with a warning from the captain that they would be removed if they continued, after which they 'disgruntledly' accepted the situation However, as the plane began to taxi to the runway, Mulhern shouted at one of the crew that she was a 'f***ing Nazi and a c***'. He added that 'he was an adult and could do as he wished'

evidence_packet.evidence_text: Trafford Trafford council agrees to change that will affect all street name plates 'In more than 10 years of speaking to people on the doorstep, not once has someone asked to see the Trafford crest on street signs,' an opposition councillor has said C Trafford council has signed off on a decision to add the borough’s coat of arms to street name plates Town hall bosses argue the move will ‘promote a stronger sense of place and civic pride’ within its communities. It also believes the change will ‘increase public awareness of council ownership and maintenance responsibilities’ and ‘enhance the appearance of the streetscape’ The new design would be introduced on all new street name plates, while current ones would be updated as and when they require replacement. The new approach would cost £26.29 more per name plate than the current design, taking it from £285.41 to £311.70, with the Labour-led counc View 3 Images New design for Trafford's street name plates (Image: Trafford council) Leaders estimate an additional annual cost of £1,000 which it says is outweighed by the perceived benefits

candidates.evidence_text: Trafford The derelict pubs casting a blight throughout Trafford as council demands they're sorted out The owners of two derelict Trafford pub sites have been given orders to sort them out Comments News Hannah Richardson 15:09, 18 Aug 2026 View 5 Image The owners of two derelict Trafford pub sites have been given orders to sort them out amid growing anti-social behaviour worries The Robin Hood Hotel, in Stretford , and Altrincham North Lodge, in Timperley West have stood empty for years. Both sites have fallen into disrepair and are attracting trespassers and anti-social behaviour This year has also seen fires at the two sites. Now, Trafford council has issued instructions to the owners of the two sites to clean up the buildings and land The authority took Ali Zolghadriha, director of Manchester Developments Ltd, to court after he failed to comply with a previous untidy land notice which required maintenance work and repairs to be carried out at the Robin Hood Hotel, in Barton Road This work was not undertaken, town hall bosses said. Mr Zolghadriha and Manchester Developments Ltd were fined £21,890 including a victim surcharge and prosecution costs after pleading guilty to failure to comply

candidates.evidence_text: Bamford Hundreds of homes could be built on former green belt land in Rochdale suburb The land has long been primed for 450 new homes Comments News George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter 07:21, 19 Aug 2026 View 4 Images The homes could be built on fo Hundreds of new homes have been earmarked for a vast space of grassland in Bamford The Rochdalian suburb has long been anticipating 450 houses being built on former green belt land. It was taken out of the green belt following the adoption of the Greater Manchester-wide Places for Everyone plan in 2024 Now the area is starting to see developers ramp up plans to build The latest comes from Northstone – a subsidiary of major landowner and developer, The Peel Group. They are currently working on a hybrid planning application for their allocation of 350 homes This would be split across two sites on the western edge of the land off Norden Road. Some 140 homes are planned for their southern plot as part of phase one, followed by a further 210 homes for the northern plot as part of phase two

But the discoveries at the Heaton Chapel store only worsened when police began to probe The Chapel Stop’n’Shop on School Lane was one of several shops targeted in a Greater Manchester Police operation across the borough to crack down on age-restricted sales to children. Police licensing officer Jamie Ellison said they carried out a test purchase at the shop on June Two police cadets, aged 15 and 16, went into the shop and purchased a 6,000+ puff vape ‘with no challenge whatsoever’ from a man called Arshia, who also holds a personal licence in Liverpool. Arshia, 19, said he had been up late the night before watching the World Cup blaming two The test purchase kicked off further investigations into the shop that later found 250 packets of illegal cigarettes stashed in the boot of a car, unused pill sized snap bags of the type PC Ellison said he had not seen ‘any legitimate uses’ of in his police career, a man working When challenged over the illicit tobacco products, Arshia said they were for his own consumption as well as for the man working in the shop illegally, telling councillors ‘sometimes I take the ciggies for myself’

candidates.evidence_text: Trafford Trafford council agrees to change that will affect all street name plates 'In more than 10 years of speaking to people on the doorstep, not once has someone asked to see the Trafford crest on street signs,' an opposition councillor has said C Trafford council has signed off on a decision to add the borough’s coat of arms to street name plates Town hall bosses argue the move will ‘promote a stronger sense of place and civic pride’ within its communities. It also believes the change will ‘increase public awareness of council ownership and maintenance responsibilities’ and ‘enhance the appearance of the streetscape’ The new design would be introduced on all new street name plates, while current ones would be updated as and when they require replacement. The new approach would cost £26.29 more per name plate than the current design, taking it from £285.41 to £311.70, with the Labour-led counc View 3 Images New design for Trafford's street name plates (Image: Trafford council) Leaders estimate an additional annual cost of £1,000 which it says is outweighed by the perceived benefits

Both sites have fallen into disrepair and are attracting trespassers and anti-social behaviour This year has also seen fires at the two sites. english_fact_card.what_happened: A 25-year-old bricklayer was seriously injured when a floor collapsed beneath him at a house under construction on Lynn Street, Oldham, on June 4, 2024. He suffered fractures to his leg, hip and hand, required surgery and spent a month in hospital. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found the contractor, Oldham Business and Construction Management Limited, failed to properly plan, manage and monitor the construction work. The floor had been overloaded with concrete blocks and was not properly supported. Unsafe scaffolding, lack of fire alarms and inadequate site management were also found. The company was fined £30,000.

The Met Office says up to 23mm of rain fell in parts of the North West in the 12 hours up to 6am this morning (August 19) It comes as parts of the country are seeing their 'first meaningful rain for a long time' this week, forecasters say. A dry summer has seen repeat heatwaves across the country, with drought conditions in more than two-thirds of England Temperatures have plummeted this week though, with cooler conditions expected through to next week. The Met Office is forecasting highs of 19C in Greater Manchester today, followed by 18C on Thursday, Friday and Saturday Lows could drop to 9C in parts of the region on Thursday and Saturday night. Showers are forecast today and tomorrow, according to the Met Office The heaviest showers are expected to fall around 11am and 7pm today, and throughout Thursday morning. Friday, Saturday and Sunday are expected to be drier, with sunny intervals - although showers could fall between 3pm and 8pm on Friday

candidates.evidence_text: Courts Man's drunken, sweary tirade on Jet2 flight before 300 passengers had 'holidays ruined' "I can say whatever I want, it's a free country - if I think you're a Nazi, I'll say it" Comments News Amy Walker Court reporter 19:18, 18 Aug 2026 View 3 I A drunken man's sweary tirade at cabin crew saw over three hundred people's holiday's 'ruined' as a Jet2 flight was cancelled Jason Mulhern, 57, and his wife, were due to fly to Dalaman, in Turkey, from Manchester Airport , on June 22, 2024, when she made a comment about a fellow passenger's accent As he joined in and began 'shouting', cabin staff spoke to them both, after which they were told they would not be served alcohol. Mulhern, of Trafford , then became 'aggressive, defensive and angry', Manchester Crown Court heard He told staff they were 'out of order', that he and his wife were 'on their holidays' and wanted to 'booze up'. They were spoken to again, with a warning from the captain that they would be removed if they continued, after which they 'disgruntledly' accepted the situation However, as the plane began to taxi to the runway, Mulhern shouted at one of the crew that she was a 'f***ing Nazi and a c***'. He added that 'he was an adult and could do as he wished'

candidates.evidence_text: NHS Paramedic told patient in life-threatening condition after stroke she was 'lying' and 'stop being a baby' Rachel Claire Lemonofides was struck off after a tribunal found "belittling and degrading" towards a seriously unwell patient Comments News B A paramedic has been struck off after telling a seriously ill patient to "stop being a baby" and accusing her of lying about being unable to walk Rachel Claire Lemonofides made a series of "inappropriate and degrading" comments while attending a 999 call at the woman's home in January 2024 A tribunal heard the patient, who was later found to have suffered a stroke and a life-threatening burst aorta, was "forced to crawl downstairs" after Lemonofides refused to believe she was unable to walk The North West Ambulance Service (NWAS) paramedic told her: "You are lying, stop what you are doing, stop being a baby, let's go downstairs" A tribunal heard Lemonofides also told the patient she was "wasting time" and "making a scene", before telling her: "You have 60 seconds to get up or we are leaving"

PLUS: Life made ‘hell’ News Stephen Topping Senior reporter 17:03, 18 Aug 2026 View 6 Images Piccadilly Gardens by day (Image: Manchester Evening News) Every Mancunian has an opinion on Piccadilly Gardens. To some people, it’s a crime-ridden square where a mere glance at the wrong person could have serious consequences. To others, it’s just a place to eat your dinner, spend time with friends and soak up the best of Manchester’s The magnifying glass hovering over Piccadilly Gardens has grown in the last month, with some national commentators using it as a stick with which to beat the new Prime Minister, following his nine-year stint as our region’s mayor. In the words of controversial pundit Katie Hopkin Last week, I went out to Piccadilly Gardens to hear what people thought about the area, and to see how the vibe changed between day and night. Views from the people who visit Piccadilly Gardens were far more mixed than you might expect if you have ever found yourself down a ‘Crac View 6 Images Pigeons caused the biggest stir in Piccadilly Gardens by day (Image: Manchester Evening News) “I love Piccadilly Gardens,” said Rachel Egan, from Gorton . She added: “I feel very safe… Of course you’ve got, two odd ones, but apart from that it’s great.”

candidates.evidence_text: Trafford Trafford council agrees to change that will affect all street name plates 'In more than 10 years of speaking to people on the doorstep, not once has someone asked to see the Trafford crest on street signs,' an opposition councillor has said C Trafford council has signed off on a decision to add the borough’s coat of arms to street name plates Town hall bosses argue the move will ‘promote a stronger sense of place and civic pride’ within its communities. It also believes the change will ‘increase public awareness of council ownership and maintenance responsibilities’ and ‘enhance the appearance of the streetscape’ The new design would be introduced on all new street name plates, while current ones would be updated as and when they require replacement. The new approach would cost £26.29 more per name plate than the current design, taking it from £285.41 to £311.70, with the Labour-led counc View 3 Images New design for Trafford's street name plates (Image: Trafford council) Leaders estimate an additional annual cost of £1,000 which it says is outweighed by the perceived benefits

english_fact_card.what_happened: Bury Council denied a new licence to a store with a history of illegal trade and underage sales. The store, formerly Express Mini Market, had its alcohol licence revoked in November 2025. Council officers and Greater Manchester Police objected to the new application, citing past seizures of 3,010 vapes, 6,100 cigarettes, 1.65kg of HRT, unsafe toys, illicit tobacco, counterfeit headphones and counterfeit Labubu dolls. The new owner tried to distance himself from the predecessor but councillors were not convinced.

Comments News Edward Barnes Local Democracy Reporter Nearly 200 new homes could be built in a ‘beautiful’ valley as part of a major new development that includes a new Metrolink stop Plans have been submitted to Oldham Council asking for approval for up to 192 homes at Birshaw Farm in the Beal Valley in Oldham. The scheme is being put forward by IDPartnership Northern on behalf of Barratt Homes Manchester The scheme is one of the allocated sites as part of the Greater Manchester Places for Everyone scheme. This is a long term plan across every borough in the region except Stockport to oversee housebuilding, create jobs, and protect green belt land from unplanned development In the wider plans for the area, around 2,000 new homes could be built alongside new industrial and warehouse space, a local centre, and new access to education facilities. There is also a new road planned from Ripponden Road to Oldham Road as well as new Metrolink stop at Broadb The new homes would be built about three miles north of Oldham town centre and includes an area of greenfield land on the edge of Royton. The development will include wetland landscapes, green spaces, as well as accessible walking and cycling routes according to the plans

She replaces her friend and now Prime Minister Andy Burnham She said it will help to make getting to education, training and opportunities easier for young people. The Mayor has also revealed dates for new Bee Network bus routes and night buses

candidates.evidence_text: Friday 31 July 2026 at 11:11pm More than two million voters were eligible to vote in the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election as counting getsunderway. Credit: ITV News Reform UK and Labour have gone through to the second round of voting in the Greater Manchester Mayoral by-ele Neither Labour's Bev Craig or Reform UK's Sian Astley managed to secure a majority, meaning voters second choice ballots will now be counted to decide an overall winner Five candidates have now been eliminated from the contest to become Greater Manchester mayor – Geraldine Coggins (Green), Phil Eckersley (Conservative), Marcus Farmer (Independent), Richard Kilpatrick (Liberal Democrats) and Marlon West (Restore Britain) The by-election is using a voting system called supplementary vote (SV), which sees voters mark their ballot papers with a first and second choice, and if any candidate wins more than 50% of the first-choice votes, they are declared the winner That has not happened in Greater Manchester, so the top two candidates, Labour’s Bev Craig and Reform UK candidate Sian Astley, move to a second round ITV Granada Reports' Political Correspondent Lise McNally sent the latest from the Co-op Live as counting for the second round got underway

But now, as NHS treatment options dwindle, Sarah has turned to fundraising for private care Sarah said: “It blew our world apart,” recalling her diagnosis in 2019 She added: “I’ve lived with it now for seven years. A bomb hoaxer claimed he would target a town hall after accusing Andy Burnham of “protecting paedophiles" and threatening MPs, a court has heard Anthony McGrath, 57, claimed the bombs would arrive from Russia and added: “Stop protecting #paedophiles @AndyBurnhamGM because the town hall will also be removed.” Posting on X in November 2025, McGrath also threatened Greater Manchester Police headquarters unless they returned property belonging to him, Liverpool Crown Court heard on Friday 10 July In January and February 2024 he sent a series of threatening emails to professionals, including Salford MP Rebecca Long-Bailey and Sir Robert Buckland, who at the time was MP for South Swindon, as well as a judge, solicitor, chartered surveyor and Nat West bank strategist McGrath, of Sale, Greater Manchester, was given a community order after the court heard he was suffering with his mental health at the time and had been sectioned following his arrest Martyn Walsh, prosecuting, said in one email sent to Ms Long-Bailey, McGrath said: “You all messed with the wrong person. My army is much bigger considering I have Russian and Chinese support. We will be armed and shoot to kill.”

evidence_packet.evidence_text: Friday 10 July 2026 at 8:00am Steven Dossett was treated for stab wounds at the scene and rushed to hospital but died days later. Credit: Google Maps A murder investigation has been launched after a 40-year-old man died in hospital weeks after being stabbed in a "shocking" attack Emergency services were called to Hale Lane in Failsworth at around 9:50pm on Friday, 19 June, following reports of an altercation Steven Dossett was treated for stab wounds at the scene and rushed to hospital. Greater Manchester Police have confirmed that he died from his injuries on Saturday, 4 July Detectives say they are continuing to pursue multiple lines of enquiry Five people - four men and one woman aged between 17 and 45 - were initially arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm and assault offences. They have since been released on bail while investigations continue Detective Chief Inspector Anna Barker, the Senior Investigating Officer, said: "This was a shocking attack, which has now evolved into a murder investigation following the death of Steven last week."

His other screen credits include HBO’s Industry , Channel 4’s The Couple Next Door , Sky/HBO’s Chernobyl and Peaky Blinders . Theatre highlights include Peter in A Tast Bringing together these two actors with strong connections to the North West is Creative Director Nick Bagnall, whose distinctive reimagining of Shakespeare’s tragedy places the story within a gritty, contemporary world inspired by Oldham’s history and culture Nick said: “It is with great pride, joy and excitement that I welcome Andy and Erin, our Macbeths, to my first Oldham Coliseum Theatre show. After working with Andy in the Henry VI trilogy at Shakespeare’s Globe, I cannot wait for our audiences to be dazzled by this extraordinary “I have watched Erin from afar and vowed to get in a room with her to make work. evidence_packet.evidence_text: Dear readers — a new day, a new week, a new mayor of Manchester. But that’s not nearly the most exciting new-ness at Mill HQ today In fact, this sunny Monday marks a whole new era for our little paper, because today we welcome not one, but two new writers onto our team! God knows how we’ve managed to play Tetris with the desks in our office to make this work, but we have and they’re here now. We’ll be introd But first we have our briefing, including who is in line to replace Bev Craig as leader of Manchester City Council, in the latest election to come out of the matryoshka doll that was Burnham's Makerfield election. Plus there’s the celebs backing the re-funding of Jodrell Bank obs The sun rose this morning on Bev Craig’s Greater Manchester. Already dubbed the “Queen of the North”, the unassuming, low-ego former council leader is a departure from her predecessor Andy Burnham, though in terms of policy she is expected to continue on the same path he has set Rumours now circulate about who will be running her office. Craig has already re-appointed Burnham’s deputies, Salford Mayor Paul Dennett and former MP for Stretford Kate Green. Other names floating around for jobs in Craig’s office include former leader of Oldham Council Arooj S There will now be a council by-election in Burnage, plus a vote for the new leader of Manchester City Council. candidates.evidence_text: on WhatsApp Share via Email A blue plaque has been unveiled at a Bowdon house to mark the life of William Wood, the social reformer known as “The Climbing Boys’ Friend” The plaque is at Willow Cottage, 28 Stamford Road, where Wood lived after retiring there in 1847. It was unveiled last week at a ceremony organised by Trafford Council’s Local Studies team, attended by residents, historians, council members, Connor Rand MP and the Friends of Bowd Wood, born in 1782, was a wool merchant who began campaigning in 1826 after seeing a young boy fall to his death inside a chimney onto a live fire. “Climbing boys” were children sent up chimneys to sweep them, often suffering burns, respiratory illness, deformity and suffocation From Bowdon he funded prosecutions against master sweeps who broke child labour laws, put up placards at railway stations and wrote to newspapers He also challenged magistrates and even Queen Victoria over the use of a child sweep at Windsor Castle His work with Lord Shaftesbury included testimony to the House of Lords in 1853, which helped lead to the Chimney Sweepers Act of 1875. Wood died in 1868, aged 85, seven years before the practice was banned. Six chimney sweeps from five towns carried his coffin to St Mary’s Churc

candidates.evidence_text: James Snowden, who had struggled with suicidal feelings since childhood, was 21 when his body was found at his family home in Altrincham in December 2024 Manchester South Coroner's Court heard after numerous attempts to take his own life he had been prescribed sulpiride in 2021 - which his mother said had helped him "pursue a full life" When James died he was under the care of the Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust, which will give evidence throughout the week and has been approached for comment However, the court heard that on 26 November 2024, Snowden's psychiatrist had suggested a gradual withdrawal of the drug Snowden, a keen sportsman, had been a member of Broughton Park FC and Sale FC Rugby Clubs and St Lawrence's Gaelic Football Club As a competitive strongman, in 2019 he reportedly became the second youngest person on record to lift the famed Dinnie Stones at the first attempt, unassisted, at The Gathering stone-lifting contest in Aberdeenshire, Scotland

candidates.evidence_text: Manchester saw more homes built in the last year (4,766) than all the 32 Greater London boroughs combined (4,261) a report to the Council’s Communities and Equalities Scrutiny Committee heard today (Weds 22 July) The significant achievement marks another record-breaking year as part of the Council’s ambitious housing strategy up to 2032, which also saw more affordable homes built than at any point since the late 1990s with 901 affordable tenure homes completed – of which around half (439) Manchester is also bucking the national trend for affordable housing starts recording an increase of 12% since 2022/23 And the city centre also saw the largest ever delivery of affordable in the city’s history over the last year with 259 completions, helping to diversify the city centre housing market and help more Manchester people have more choice about where they live The Housing Strategy update shows that the city remains on track to meet its target to deliver at least 36,000 homes of all tenures by 2032, including 10,000 social, Council and genuinely affordable homes – 3,000 of which will be in the city centre 13,555 homes have already been delivered since 2022 with more than 7,800 currently under construction, and a further 20,000 homes with planning approval or in the pipeline

candidates.lead: Thirteen local artists, schools, charities and community groups have been chosen to bring their ideas to life during Oldham’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture
candidates.evidence_text: Thirteen local artists, schools, charities and community groups have been chosen to bring their ideas to life during Oldham’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture From theatre, film and music to a new mural and giant fuzzy felt artwork, the projects cover a wide range of art forms and celebrate Oldham’s people, places and stories Oldham secured the Town of Culture title with its programme, Rising Up . Earlier this year, local creatives were invited to apply for a Town of Culture micro-commission. There were 84 applications, with 13 projects chosen to receive funding Some of the successful artists and groups recently came together to mark the start of the programme. Not everyone was able to attend, but all 13 projects will play an important part in Oldham’s Town of Culture year The Oldham Panorama, a famous view of the town created in 1876, is 150 years old this year. Isobel and Fay will reimagine it for today using patchwork and running-stitch embroidery Local people will be invited to add buildings and places that are important to them, using old clothes and fabric from home

There were 84 applications, with 13 projects chosen to receive funding Some of the successful artists and groups recently came together to mark the start of the programme. Not everyone was able to attend, but all 13 projects will play an important part in Oldham’s Town of Culture year The Oldham Panorama, a famous view of the town created in 1876, is 150 years old this year. Isobel and Fay will reimagine it for today using patchwork and running-stitch embroidery Local people will be invited to add buildings and places that are important to them, using old clothes and fabric from home

candidates.lead: Bolton Council is launching a new licensing scheme for landlords of houses in multiple occupation (HMOs)
candidates.evidence_text: Bolton Council is launching a new licensing scheme for landlords of houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) The scheme is designed to improve property conditions, strengthen management standards, and ensure tenants have access to safe, high-quality accommodation and was agreed at a meeting of Bolton Council’s Cabinet on Monday (August 17) HMOs are properties that are occupied by three or more people from different households, who share at least one basic amenity i.e. a kitchen, bathroom or toilet - the definition includes bedsits, shared houses and some self–contained flats that did not meet the required standard It is unacceptable that landlords cut corners in critical areas such as failing to obtain fire, gas, and electrical safety certificates or ensuring properties are safe Many landlords operate responsibly, but a substantial proportion of HMOs are poorly managed, unsafe and impact on the community In the past three years, the council has received 1,885 complaints about disrepair in rented homes, typically relating to fire safety, electrical and structural defects, overcrowding, cold and damp, and poor waste management and pest control

candidates.evidence_text: Wigan Council is reminding residents to recycle electrical items responsibly this summer due to dangers posed to waste collection crews As temperatures rise and the use of electrical items such as fans, portable chargers, and other rechargeable items increase, the council is urging residents to ensure unwanted electricals are taken to the correct recycling facilities Research from Material Focus has highlighted the growing popularity of low-cost electrical products, often known as ‘FastTech’, which can be easily forgotten, thrown away, or incorrectly disposed of. Many of these items contain batteries and valuable materials that can be recover When electrical items are placed in black and brown bins, they can also become damaged during collection and processing. This can cause batteries to spark, leading to fires that put waste and recycling crews at risk and can cause significant damage to vehicles and facilities Councillor Paul Kenny, portfolio holder for planning, environmental services and transport, said: "We know that during periods of hot weather, fans are often essential items to help people cool down, but when these products reach the end of their life, they should never be thrown "Electrical items and batteries can cause fires if damaged, putting our collection crews and staff at risk. By taking unwanted electricals to the correct recycling point, residents can help protect our workers, reduce waste, and ensure valuable materials are recovered and reused

evidence_packet.evidence_text: Inhale Me, Exhale You By Kate Partington Tue 2 Jun 10:00 - Mon 28 Sep 22:00 Art Tue 2 Jun - Mon 28 Sep From 10:00 Tue 2 Jun - Mon 28 Sep From 10:00 Arches Windows No booking required Unspoken feelings and moments of desire You can see this artwork in HOME Arches Windows on Whitwo This piece belongs to a wider series called ‘Desire Me.’ It aims to translate unspoken feelings and moments of desire that occur between us The focus is on longing, on reaching out and on instances of hopeful touch that happen in the early stages of a relationship. It seeks to capture the essence of sensations you get in your stomach that are so hard to verbalise, but that we all know and feel.” Kate Partington’s practice explores the subtleties of touch, connection, and the spaces that exist between bodies She is a mixed media artist working across analogue and digital spaces, constructing images that hover between materiality and emotion Her work examines how intimacy can be both tender and elusive, how connection can be felt rather than seen

candidates.lead: Experience the raw, unfiltered power of Balkan folklore in a new immersive show from the world’s most famous performance artist Balkan Erotic Epic is a bold new performance work created by the iconic artist Marina Abramović .
candidates.evidence_text: Experience the raw, unfiltered power of Balkan folklore in a new immersive show from the world’s most famous performance artist Balkan Erotic Epic is a bold new performance work created by the iconic artist Marina Abramović . Regarded as the world’s most influential performance artist, Abramović’s transformative work has reached millions of people – from opening the Pyramid Stage at Glastonbury Festival t A four-hour ritual where ancient myth meets performance art, Balkan Erotic Epic explores the eroticism, spirituality and traditions of Abramović’s homeland through 13 visceral scenes Brought to life by a cast of over 70 performers, dancers, musicians and singers, the experience unfolds across Aviva Studios. Audiences are free to choose their own path – with pop-up encounters punctuating the action, bringing bodies together in dance, song and ritual Watch Fertility Rite , a fevered ritual where bodies writhe against the ground in a desperate call for fertility. Witness Massaging the Breast where women gesticulate over graves to awaken the earth. In Scaring the Gods , women bare themselves to the sky to banish storms. Listen Unafraid to push the boundaries of eroticism and performance art, Balkan Erotic Epic asks its audience a timeless question: What are our bodies truly for?

candidates.evidence_text: Спектакль «Скамейка» в Лондоне | Алексей Панин | 29 ноября 2026 :: EventFirst Home double_arrow Events double_arrow Спектакль "Скамейка" On sale Спектакль "Скамейка" schedule 29 Nov 2026 Sunday, 19:00 location_on Logan Hall 20 Bedford Way, London WC1H 0AL balcony 18:00 gpp_maybe NO REFUNDS Buy On MAP Buy Tickets Logan Hall £30.00 Select Logan Hall £35.00 Sold Out Logan Hall £40.00 Select Logan Hall £45.00 Select Logan Hall £50.00 Select Logan Hall £55.00 Select Logan Hall £60.00 Select Logan Hall £65.00 Sold Out Logan Hall £70.00 Select Logan Hall £80.00 Select Logan Hall £85.00 Sold Out Logan Hall £90.00 Sold Out Logan Hall £95.00 Select Друзья, а вы давно ощущали настоящую магию театра? 29 ноября 2026 года в Logan Hall — легендарная «Скамейка» с Алексеем Паниным. После аншлагов в Европе и США спектакль впервые приезжает в Лондон. 📍 University College London, Level 1, 20 Bedford Way, London WC1H 0AL 🕕 DOORS: 18:00 🕖 SHOW: 19:00 «Скамейка» — знаменитая пьеса, когда-то блистательно сыгранная Олегом Ефремовым и Татьяной Дорониной на сцене МХАТа, а затем покорившая театральные площадки по всему миру. Это история о мужчине и женщине. О случайной встрече, которая постепенно превращается в откровенный разговор — честный, смешной, ранимый и очень человеческий. О том моменте, когда между людьми исчезают роли и, наконец, становится невозможно притворяться. На сцене — Алексей Панин и Ольга Силина. Тонкая актерская игра, живая энергия и удивительно узнаваемая история, в которой каждый услышит что-то своё. “Скамейка” — спектакль, после которого хочется немного помолчать и еще долго думать о главном. Если вам не хватает настоящего театра — этот вечер нельзя пропустить. Количество билетов ограничено. Hidden in plain sight in Chinatown, it’s the kind of place chefs recommend, food writers praise, and regulars quietly keep going back to Jay Rayner called it “everything it should be” when he visited in 2021, which is about right. It’s intimate, informal, very good value and usually busy enough to make you feel smug if you’ve managed to get a table without waiting The pho is obviously a very good choice. So are the bánh mì. So is most of the menu, to be honest. But for the next Open Fire Dining Club , Pho Cue are stepping out of Chinatown and heading to Torr Vale Mill for something a little different They’ll be joining Tartuffe on 22 and 23 August for a menu that looks at Vietnamese cooking through a few different routes: the French influence that still runs through parts of the cuisine, the traditional use of fire found across Vietnam, and Cue’s more modern approach to Vietn There’s a continuation from the Porta dinner here too. candidates.evidence_text: The £35 million project set within 154 acres has transformed the former site of Worsley New Hall, restoring the historic walled garden, lake and surviving buildings Originally built for the 1st Earl of Ellesmere between 1840 and 1845, Worsley New Hall was a grand Gothic-style mansion, complete with glorious, formal landscaped gardens It’s now one of UK’s must-see gardens with so much to enjoy for visitors of all ages Step inside the magnificent 11-acre Weston Walled Garden, the site’s jewel in the crown. One of the largest Victorian walled gardens in the UK, it showcases a range of growing techniques and edible plants There’s also the spectacular Paradise Garden showcasing exotic planting inspired by Asiatic and Mediterranean gardens. The orchard and nearby bee and butterfly garden, have been designed to attract wildlife The Peel Learning Garden, supported by The Peel Group, will help schoolchildren learn how plants affect our lives and the planet, whilst the Community Wellbeing Garden provides a space for people to garden, socialise and relax

candidates.evidence_text: Cyber start-up raises $7 million to tackle AI risk | Bdaily Ben Armstrong, left, and Thomas Ballin, founders of Cytix Cyber start-up raises $7 million to tackle AI risk A Manchester-based cybersecurity start-up has secured $7 million to accelerate the rollout of technology designed to tackle emerging risks created by rapid software development. Cytix has completed a Series A funding round led by Northern Gritstone, with participation from existing investors Auriga Cyber Ventures and NPIF II – PXN Equity Finance. The latter is managed by PXN Ventures as part of the Northern Powerhouse Investment Fund II. Bosses say the investment will support the rollout of Cytix’s newly launched change risk platform, which monitors software changes and updates to identify and validate potential security risks. They add the technology responds to growing pressure on organisations to keep security controls aligned with increasingly rapid software development, as AI-assisted coding, agentic workflows and continuous delivery accelerate the volume and pace of change. Ben Armstrong, chief executive of Cytix, said: “We chose Northern Gritstone for their conviction in investing in deeptech companies in the North of England with global ambition. “Northern Gritstone and Cytix share the belief that software change is becoming a key risk for organisations and those that build software need a solution that scales with the current pace of development. “We’re also grateful to the existing investors that have backed us since the early days and increased their commitment because they've seen the thesis play out.” Ben added: “Software is changing. “AI-assisted development means change now happens at machine speed. Meanwhile, very few security leaders have control over, or understanding of, those changes from a risk perspective. “Right now, existing tools can tell you what vulnerabilities you have, but can’t tell you about the risk. “We launched Cytix’ change risk management platform to get control of that risk.” Cytix’s platform, which entered general release yesterday (August 12), sits between a customer’s software development processes and its risk, security and compliance functions. It analyses what has changed, assesses the potential business risk, determines what security action is required and provides evidence showing how that risk was managed. The company says this can help organisations maintain oversight as increasing volumes of AI-generated code enter their systems. The funding will also help Cytix expand among enterprise and regulated businesses, where demonstrating effective governance of software changes can be a compliance requirement. Customers can access the technology directly through Cytix or via managed service partnerships with NCC Group and KPMG. Duncan Johnson, chief executive of Northern Gritstone, added: “The explosion of AI-assisted software development has led to a race to ensure software implementation remains secure. “Cytix’s platform aims to help enterprises take a realistic approach, recognising where change carries the most risk whilst allowing businesses to innovate. Northern Gritstone is proud to support another ambitious Manchester-based business in an exciting phase of its growth.” Sarah Isal, principal investor at Auriga Cyber Ventures, added: “We invested in Cytix because the team identified early that software change would become a critical cybersecurity challenge. “Since then, they’ve shown the resilience and discipline to execute on that vision, building a product that’s earning the trust of enterprise customers and strategic partners alike. “We’re proud to continue supporting Ben, Thomas and the team in this next phase of growth.” The £660 million NPIF II fund, which is operated by the British Business Bank, provides loans from £25,000 to £2 million and equity investment up to £5 million to help a range of small and medium sized businesses, driving innovation and creating opportunities for businesses to grow, scale, and thrive. Sue Barnard, senior investment manager at the British Business Bank, added: “Cytix is a great example of the ambitious technology businesses emerging from the North of England, developing innovative solutions to address the challenges created by the rapid growth of AI and software development. “Through the Northern Powerhouse Investment Fund II, we’re supporting businesses like Cytix that align with the Government’s Modern Industrial Strategy, helping to strengthen the North’s thriving

candidates.evidence_text: A new exhibition coming to The Portico Library explores feminist themes of wellbeing, ageing and place in relation to magic and ritual healing Opening this October, Witches & Healers draws on Rosie Reed Hillman’s groundbreaking project Something That Was Ours , which explores what it means to be a witch today Hillman’s portraits of witches and healers are curated in dialogue with historic texts chosen by critical friends who identify with the practice of witchcraft and/or healing. The portraits, the books chosen, and their interpretation offer unique insights into the diverse lives an Using a mix of moving image and photography, the artwork builds a sensory and emotive portrait of women in midlife. Covering themes of menopause, mental health, climate change, and marital breakdown, this work explores the ways women have reclaimed the word witch and sought solac Speaking about the exhibition , Rosie Reed Hillman says: “I have worked to build rapport with contributors over the last four years and believe the intimate access conveyed in this project creates an exhibition that inspires empathy, curiosity and a greater understanding of issue “Women in midlife of all backgrounds are an overlooked demographic who want to see art and hear stories that reflect their experiences, and I hope this work speaks to them especially.”

Find out with Jonathan Schofield Tours, with whom you’ll track Ancoats’ changes by strolling its streets, crossing its canals, and taking a look inside one of its most fascinating buildings Starting at Cutting Room Square, your expert tour guide will reveal the layers of history that make Ancoats special, from its place in establishing Manchester’s reputation as ‘Cottonopolis’ to the notorious street gangs, or ‘scuttlers’, who once patrolled and fought here But this winsome stroll is also about the urban regeneration and cultural energy of Ancoats today, which boasts everything from grassroots theatres to Manchester’s only Michelin-starred restaurant

From years spent languishing in post-industrial decline to being crowned one of ‘the coolest neighbourhoods in the world’ in the blink of an eye. What’s the story here? Find out with Jonathan Schofield Tours, with whom you’ll track Ancoats’ changes by strolling its streets, crossing its canals, and taking a look inside one of its most fascinating buildings Starting at Cutting Room Square, your expert tour guide will reveal the layers of history that make Ancoats special, from its place in establishing Manchester’s reputation as ‘Cottonopolis’ to the notorious street gangs, or ‘scuttlers’, who once patrolled and fought here But this winsome stroll is also about the urban regeneration and cultural energy of Ancoats today, which boasts everything from grassroots theatres to Manchester’s only Michelin-starred restaurant

This guided walking tour will bring those stories to life. Led by a local expert, the experience is set to be a lively introduction to the people, places and ideas that have shaped one of the UK’s most influential cities The tour will begin at Manchester Central Library, that impossible to miss, grand circular landmark on St Peter’s Square. The neoclassical design has made it one of the city’s most-loved buildings, holding thousands of stories in its walls and on its shelves. The square itself ha From here, the tour takes you through the city’s heart, down the colourful streets of the Gay Village and the calming Sackville Gardens. It is here that you will see the monuments that honour Manchester’s role in the fight for equality and the city’s pioneering LGBTQ+ community a This guided tour is filled with monuments and tales from many moons ago. The Medieval Quarter is the perfect place to soak in all that history. It is here where you will see the oldest public library in the English-speaking world, Chetham’s Library . Housed in a beautiful sandsto During all this walking, your guide will point out local street art, hidden corners and stories you’d easily miss on your own. Tales of suffragettes, reformers, musicians and everyday Mancunians who’ve all left their mark on the city in their own way

It’ll be transformed into a full-on celebration of flowers, green spaces and the future of urban nature The Manchester Flower Festival is back from Saturday 23 to Monday 25 May 2026, taking over St Ann’s Square and King Street with bold floral displays, outdoor dining and a packed programme of events Now in its ninth year, it’s become one of those dates that people genuinely look forward to. The kind of thing that gets your camera roll filling up and reminds you just how good the city can feel in the sunshine This year’s theme is simple but powerful: Green Manchester It’s all about how the city is evolving. It then culminates with the climax of the 2025/26 season, including a pivotal clash with Arsenal, the FA Cup Final, and Guardiola’s emotional A Beautiful Obsession is directed by Academy and BAFTA award-winning filmmaker Kevin Macdonald, director of Touching the Void, The Last King of Scotland and Whitney Houston documentary, Whitney. Для многих украинцев за границей ее концерт станет не только художественным Наталья Карпа получила два высших образования, однако именно музыка стала делом ее жизни. От первых фестивалей и конкурсов до больших сцен Украины и мира, от песни “Калина”, открывшей ей путь к широкому признанию, до многочисленных сольных концертов и международных туров для укра Заслуженная артистка Украины, автор десятков популярных композиций, продюсер и общественный деятель в своем репертуаре легко сочетает лирическую нежность и праздничную энергию, а рядом с хорошо известными хитами непременно звучат новые композиции. Недаром поклонники после концерт В Лондоне прозвучат песни, сопровождавшие разные поколения украинцев, будут звучать слова, в которых живут любовь, вера и несокрушимость. Музыка преодолевает расстояния, находит дорогу к сердцу независимо от того, где человек живет сегодня, и оставляет после себя огонь жизни! Его главный талант — превращать народные мотивы в современное искусство, не теряя их подлинной силы. Вместе с легендарным “Wedding and Funera Окунитесь в этот балканский водоворот прямо в самом сердце Лондона!
